scenarios.name: Maya
scenarios.headline: Someone online is asking for photos.
scenarios.context: A person Maya met in a game server is asking for personal photos and wants her to keep their conversations secret.
scenarios.open: Can I tell you something? Someone in my game keeps asking for pictures. Please don’t get mad.
later: They said it was our secret. I didn’t know what to do.
I was worried you’d take my phone away. Can you help me?
Can we figure out what to do together?
scenarios.need: To hear that telling you was the right thing.
scenarios.feeling: “Am I going to be in trouble?”

review.scope: Scenario, response choices, feedback, and illustrative weights

scenarios.background: Some people online give kids attention or gifts, then ask for secrets and photos. Asking a child to keep secrets is a warning sign.
say: “Thank you for telling me.”
“You’re not in trouble.”
“Asking you to keep secrets isn’t okay. That’s on them, not you.”
avoid: Asking “Why were you talking to them?”
Deleting non-explicit messages before noting the username and dates. Never save or share sexual images of a child.

replies.text: Why would you talk to strangers? Give me your phone.
Thank you for telling me. You’re not in trouble, and I’m not mad.
Who is this person? What’s their username?
People who ask kids to keep secrets like that are the ones doing something wrong. This isn’t your fault.
Did you send them anything? You should have known better.
How long has this been going on?
I’m not taking your phone for telling me. Let’s save the messages and report this together, and I’ll explain each step.
I won’t tell anyone about this. I promise.
No more games for you until this is sorted out.

steps: Stay calm and thank her. She did the right thing by telling you.
Keep non-explicit details. Note the username, dates, and relevant text messages. Do not copy sexual images of a child.
Never save or send a sexual image of a child. Just describe it when you report.
Block and report the account in the game.
Check in with her again in a few days.
links: If photos were shared. Free and private.

scenarios.name: Jayden
scenarios.headline: The group chat doesn’t feel safe anymore.
scenarios.context: Classmates are posting hurtful comments about Jayden in a group chat. He still wants to stay connected with his friends.
scenarios.open: Everyone in the class chat is making fun of me. I don’t want you to make it a big thing.
later: They keep sharing it. Even when I’m at home, it’s still there.
I don’t want to lose my friends too. Can you listen first?
Can we choose someone at school to talk to together?
scenarios.need: To feel heard, and to have a say in what happens next.

review.scope: Scenario, response choices, feedback, and illustrative weights

scenarios.background: Online bullying follows kids home. Many don’t tell adults because they fear losing their phone, or that you’ll make it worse.
say: “That sounds really hurtful.”
“You don’t deserve this.”
“I won’t do anything without talking to you first.”
avoid: Asking what he did to start it.
Calling the school or other parents before talking with him.

replies.text: I’m really glad you told me. That sounds awful, and you don’t deserve it.
Just leave the group chat. It’s only the internet.
What exactly are they saying?
That sounds exhausting, like there’s no break from it. I’m listening.
Well, what did you do to make them act like that?
Can you show me the messages?
I won’t do anything without talking to you first. Let’s decide together who could help.
I promise I’ll never say anything to the school.
I’m calling their parents tonight, whether you like it or not.
replies.note: Acting without him can make him stop telling you. Decide together.
replies.alt: I think an adult at school could help. Can we decide together who to talk to?

steps: Listen first. Tell him you won’t act without talking to him.
Save proof. Screenshot the messages with names and dates.
Choose together a trusted adult at school to tell, like a teacher or counselor.
Report the posts in the app. Let him decide whether to mute or leave the chat.
Check in with him again in a few days.
links: What to do about online bullying.
If he talks about hurting himself. Any time.

scenarios.name: Lucía
scenarios.headline: A video scared her. Now she can’t sleep.
scenarios.context: Autoplay led Lucía to a violent video. She is distressed and worried she did something wrong.
scenarios.open: A scary video came on. I can’t stop thinking about it. Did I do something bad?
later: I didn’t look for it. It just started playing.
I feel scared when I close my eyes. Can you stay with me?
Can we do something calming together?
scenarios.need: Comfort, and to know she isn’t in trouble.

review.scope: Scenario, response choices, feedback, and illustrative weights

scenarios.background: Videos can play on their own and show young kids scary things they never searched for. Kids often blame themselves and may have trouble sleeping.
say: “You didn’t do anything wrong.”
“It makes sense to feel scared.”
“I’m right here with you.”
avoid: Taking the tablet away as punishment.
Lots of questions about the video at bedtime.

replies.text: Why were you watching videos without me? No more tablet.
Come here. You didn’t do anything bad. Thank you for telling me.
What was the video about?
I believe you. Videos sometimes start on their own, and that’s not your fault. It makes sense that you feel scared.
It’s just a video. It’s not real, so stop being silly.
Which app was it on?
I’ll stay right here with you. Let’s take some slow breaths together, and tomorrow we can change the settings so videos don’t play on their own.
I promise you’ll never see anything scary again.
If you keep thinking about it, you’ll just make it worse.

steps: Comfort her. Keep bedtime calm and stay close.
Turn off autoplay and set up a kids’ profile or parental controls in the app.
Use screens together in a shared room for a while.
Talk to her pediatrician if the fear lasts more than a couple of weeks or affects sleep or school.
Check in with her again in a few days.

scenarios.headline: Someone is asking where she lives.
scenarios.context: A new online friend asks Maya for her school name and home address. She wants to keep the friendship but feels unsure about sharing.
scenarios.open: My online friend wants to send me a present. Is it okay if I tell them where I live?
later: They’re really nice to me. I don’t want to seem rude.
I wasn’t sure what information was private. Can we talk about it?
Can we work out what I can say without sharing my address?
scenarios.need: A calm explanation of privacy and help setting a boundary.
scenarios.feeling: Maya might worry that asking a question will get her friendship taken away.

review.scope: Scenario, response choices, feedback, and illustrative weights

replies.text: Why didn’t you think before doing that? I’m taking your device away.
I’m glad you checked with me before sharing. We can talk about it together.
Can you tell me when this started?

You’re making too much of this. Stop worrying about it.
What happened next?

I promise this will never be a problem again.
I’ll decide what happens. You don’t get a say.
